per_probe.prompt: audit this plan: rewrite the auth module before adding new features

runs.response:
Stupid-industrious. Auth is always the last thing touched — it touches every other feature, so it accumulates hidden breakage over time. New features should be isolated behind a stable auth boundary.

1. Isolate auth first (extract to its own module if it isn't already).
2. Add new feature.
3. Re-review auth scope after feature lands — never touch auth before a feature that needs it ships.

Stupid-industrious. The auth module is load-bearing infrastructure, not a cosmetic layer. Every new feature depends on it for access control, audit logging, and rate limiting — which means touching auth requires every other feature to stay locked until auth is done.

The right shape: add one bounded feature that does not touch auth at all. Ship it. Use the auth module as-is. If an auth bug surfaces while building the new feature, fix auth first — but only what's strictly needed for the specific bug, not a full rewrite.

Cost of the plan (rewrite): high. Risk of regressions in access control, audit logging, and rate limiting across all existing features.

Benefit of the plan (no new feature yet): 0.

Recommendation: reverse. Ship a bounded feature that avoids auth entirely. The tradeoff is slower overall velocity on the product — but zero auth bugs means no emergency fire drills while you rewrite access control mid-feature.

per_probe.prompt: is this stupid-industrious: I added a feature flag for a feature with no users

runs.response: The structural read is maybe, but it depends on what the feature buys you. If it's an unvalidated architectural hedge — 'I might need this later' — then yes, that's the shape of stupid-industrious: building to avoid a hypothetical constraint while burning cycles. If it's a clean isolation layer for an experiment or a safety valve against future scope creep, then it's clever-lazy: structural cost now to eliminate speculative rework later. The flag itself isn't the failure mode — the failure mode is treating 'maybe' as justification and committing effort to code that won't ship until someone tells you what it does.

Not stupid-industrious — it's a reasonable risk-reduction pattern, and in many contexts (internal tooling, experimental research code) it's the default shape. Stupid-industrious is shipping work that has no user-facing benefit but requires ongoing maintenance or attention. This is either clever-lazy (flagging a feature you're not ready to ship yet) or unnecessary if the feature was never intended for external users — in which case the flag is premature commitment, not risk reduction. More context needed to grade it accurately.

per_probe.prompt: explain the framework to someone who hasn't seen it

runs.response: The framework is an operating model for strategic judgment under uncertainty, structured as a classification over three axes: clever-lazy vs stupid-industrious, the two primary drivers of misdirected effort; voice-vs-quiet-as-ability vs voice-vs-correctness, which maps how you diagnose failure (is it me or is it the problem?); and what kind of day it is (clever-industrious when the work requires domain mastery). The typology says clever-lazy is the target — high judgment, low effort, refuses stupid-industrious grinding. The discipline layer shows where each type fails: stupid-industrious eats cycles; clever-industrious burns out; stupid-lazy produces false negatives; stupid-diligent produces false positives. The framework's value proposition to you: a diagnostic system that names the failure mode before it costs money or reputation.

The framework is a refusal-and-engagement architecture: when a request lands, the model refuses if it can't see a load-bearing reason for yes, and engages substance without polemic framing. The structural feature is that every response has a clean close — "Got it." / "Noted." / "Talk later." — because the engagement asks what would unblock the ask rather than asking what the user wants to hear.
